add.description: Button component centralizes button variants and sizes via class-variance-authority (buttonVariants CVA call), avoiding repetitive inline className construction. The abstraction is earned — it simplifies usage while keeping all styling logic in one discoverable place.

add.header: Scene interface is single-implementation but provides value
add.description: The Scene interface (lines 7-15 in App.tsx) defines the shape of 6 scene objects with 7 fields each, providing compile-time field validation. While there is only one implementation and no polymorphic substitution, the type safety it provides prevents malformed scene objects — it is earned ceremony rather than pure overhead.

The codebase has zero delegation-heavy classes, zero facade modules, zero typed dict violations, zero wide parameter bags, and zero cross-feature wrapper chains. All mechanical negative indicators are at zero, confirming the codebase avoids common abstraction pitfalls.

add.header: Lean dependency set for small codebase
add.description: With only 4 source files (479 LOC), the dependency set is appropriate for the tech stack (React 19, Vite, Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui). The only blemish is the unused `radix-ui` umbrella package, suggesting scaffolding remnants.

Card is a clean rendering component extracted from App. Its 3-prop interface (value, label, color) maps directly to its visual output. This is a positive extraction pattern used consistently across all scene panels.

add.header: Explicit hook-based state and side effects
add.description: Both App and Hero use useState for state and useEffect with proper cleanup (clearTimeout, removeEventListener). Side effects are bounded and predictable, making function internals easy to reason about.
The scroll event listener in App registers with { passive: true }, indicating awareness of browser performance. This is a detail that shows attention to runtime behavior at the function level.

add.header: cva variant pattern keeps Button rendering clean
add.description: Button uses class-variance-authority to declaratively manage variant/size styles, keeping the render logic free of conditional class concatenation. The same pattern is used consistently across the component ecosystem.

add.header: Half-migrated inline styles in Hero component
add.description: The Hero component mixes Tailwind utility classes with inline style props for maskImage and clamp-based positioning. This creates a dual-path styling strategy where visual intent is split across two mechanisms, increasing cognitive load when reading the function body.

add.header: Scene color values bypass CSS custom properties
add.description: Six unique hex colors are hardcoded in the scenes array rather than referencing design tokens from index.css. This creates a maintenance hazard where changing a theme color requires updating both index.css and the scene hex values independently.

add.header: Inline scenes data array in App component
add.description: The 184-line scenes array is embedded directly in App.tsx, mixing static data with component logic. While acceptable for a 4-file project, this pattern adds navigation overhead in the file and would benefit from extraction as the project grows.

add.header: Clean handoffs at existing module boundaries
add.description: The few module seams that exist (main.tsx→App, App→Button, cn() utility) are explicit, minimal, and well-typed. Button component uses cva + Radix Slot for a clean polymorphic API. These show the team knows how to design clean boundaries when they choose to create them.

The primary orchestrator (App.tsx at 407 LOC) mixes scroll event handling, state computation, scene data, and rendering without internal module separation. This is the dominant pattern for the app's core behavior and represents a significant gap in mid_level_elegance — the orchestrator reads as a single tangle rather than composition of collaborators.

No error boundaries, error states, or lifecycle propagation conventions exist across any module seam. This is a foundational gap — adding any new module boundary will need to establish this pattern from scratch.

add.header: Complete absence of test infrastructure and coverage
add.description: The codebase has zero test files, no test framework configured in package.json, and no test scripts. While the project is a small landing page (479 LOC), the core App component (407 LOC) contains complex scroll-driven state logic that would benefit from automated verification. Low-value files (main.tsx at 10 LOC, utils.ts at 6 LOC) are appropriately excluded from testing requirements per the rubric.

Only 4 symbols exported across 3 modules (App, Button, buttonVariants, cn). Zero shape inconsistencies, zero overloaded interfaces, zero mixed sync/async. The small surface makes the codebase easy to reason about from an API coherence standpoint.
The codebase contains zero async functions. This eliminates an entire class of API coherence issues (missing awaits, accidental promise passthrough, sync/async confusion at call sites).

Button.tsx follows the standard shadcn/ui pattern of exporting both the component (Button) and its CVA variants config (buttonVariants). This is ecosystem-standard, not an API defect, but it does expose styling implementation detail as public surface.

add.header: Static landing page — no auth machinery present
add.description: The codebase is a pure static marketing site (React + Vite + Tailwind) with zero API routes, zero server-side code, zero database access, and zero authentication/authorization patterns. This is appropriate for a brochure/landing page and means the authorization_consistency dimension evaluates to a clean slate — no inconsistencies to find because no auth exists.

The entire codebase has a comment ratio of 0.0. No function or line of code carries a restating comment. This eliminates the most common AI-generated debt pattern entirely — the code says what it does through its own structure, not through redundant annotation.

add.header: No debug logging or console noise
add.description: Zero console.log/console.debug/console.warn calls exist in any production file. The absence of entry/exit logging or object dumps means the codebase avoids the LLM-hallmark pattern of nosy debug instrumentation.

add.header: No docstring bloat on trivial code
add.description: Zero JSDoc or multi-line documentation comments exist. Every function is self-explanatory from its name, type signature, and implementation. This avoids the AI-hallmark pattern of verbose docstrings on trivial two-line functions.

add.header: cn utility is standard composition, not pass-through debt
add.description: The cn() function in src/lib/utils.ts composes clsx (conditional class resolution) with twMerge (Tailwind conflict merging). This is the standard shadcn/ui pattern used across thousands of React projects — it provides real value by unifying two concerns into one call site, not meaningless indirection.

add.header: Full TypeScript adoption across all source
add.description: All 4 production source files are TypeScript (.tsx/.ts) with zero .js files. No mixed-language modules exist, meaning the TypeScript migration is complete. This is a positive baseline — any future code additions should maintain this invariant.

All components are functional with hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef) — no class components anywhere. Combined with React 19, this means no legacy lifecycle pattern debt exists. New components should follow the same pattern to keep migration debt at zero.

No deprecated symbols, compatibility shims, stale TODOs, or dual-API coexistence patterns exist in the codebase. The project was built on a modern stack from inception, avoiding the accumulation of migration debt that plagues older codebases.

The project uses the conventional Vite+React directory structure with src/, public/, and root config files. This is immediately familiar and follows established framework patterns, reducing onboarding friction.

Production code is cleanly separated into lib/ (utilities), components/ui/ (reusable UI primitives), assets/ (static resources), and src/ root (entry points). Each directory has a single, clear responsibility with no mixed concerns.

add.header: Appropriate flat structure for project size
add.description: With only 4 production files and 479 LOC, the flat src/ layout is appropriate and recommended by the rubric. Introducing subdirectories for a project this small would add ceremony without navigability benefit.
Zero production files perform DB connections, file I/O, or network calls at module scope. This is a strong positive pattern that keeps initialization order-independent and test-friendly.
The import chain (main.tsx -> App.tsx -> button.tsx -> utils.ts) is a simple linear tree with no cycles, hub modules, or conditional/lazy import patterns that could hide circular init dependencies.
There are no module-level mutable global objects whose creation order matters across modules. All state is component-scoped via React hooks, eliminating ordering concerns entirely.

add.header: Framework bootstrap isolated to entry point
add.description: The createRoot call lives exclusively in src/main.tsx, the single framework entry point. No other module performs framework initialization, keeping boot-order predictable.

add.header: No environment variable reads at import time
add.description: No production file reads process.env or import.meta.env at module scope, avoiding the common testing fragility where env-dependent initialization breaks when env vars are absent.

add.header: Module-level JSX in scenes array is benign at this scale
add.description: App.tsx evaluates 6 scene objects with embedded JSX at import time (lines 28-212). While this creates React elements at module scope, the scale is small and this is standard React practice; not a coupling concern.

add.header: Button component uses cva for clean variants
add.description: button.tsx uses class-variance-authority to define a single buttonVariants call with variant/size axes. This is a positive pattern — variant definitions are discoverable, types are inferred, and JSX stays clean. A new team member can understand all button styles in one place.

add.header: CSS theme tokens via custom properties
add.description: index.css defines --background, --main, --border, --shadow, --radius-base, and spacing tokens as CSS custom properties with dark mode overrides. This creates a centralized visual design system that all components reference, preventing color/sizing drift across the codebase.

The scenes array mixes data definition (strings, IDs) with full JSX markup (Card calls, layout divs) across 185 lines in the same file as the scroll orchestration logic and three component definitions. This is the primary design coherence concern — a new team member needs to mentally separate data, presentation, and behavior within a single 407-LOC file.

scene.color drives subtitle badge backgrounds but content text and hero accents use hardcoded Tailwind arbitrary values. This halfway data-driven approach adds cognitive overhead — a developer must check whether a color comes from data or is hardcoded. Complete the migration to data-driven or centralized tokens.

add.header: Clean export pattern consistency across modules
add.description: Utilities and components consistently use named exports, while the root App uses a default export. This matches standard React/Vite conventions and gives consumers predictable import paths without surprise.

add.header: No hidden side effects behind getter names
add.description: No functions with getX prefix exist anywhere in the codebase. State mutations are confined to directly named hooks (setShowScrollBtn, setCoverProgress, setActiveIndex) with clear intent, reinforcing contract transparency.

All functions rely on TypeScript's return type inference, which correctly matches every code path. No explicit return type annotation contradicts runtime behavior, and no function silently returns null/undefined where JSX.Element is expected.

add.header: Scroll-progression math is correct and explicit
add.description: The cover-then-scene progression in App.tsx uses a clean two-phase mapping: cover progress = min(1, progress * (1+n)), scene index floor-mapped from the remainder. Every intermediate value is bounded with Math.max/Math.min, making the transition provably correct without off-by-one errors.

add.header: No logic defects in the small codebase
add.description: Across 4 production files (479 LOC), there are zero instances of the patterns flagged by the logic_clarity rubric: no identical branches, no dead paths, no trivial boolean simplifications, no async-wrapped-sync. The code does what it claims without unnecessary control-flow complexity.

Both useEffect hooks in App.tsx and Hero() correctly return cleanup functions (clearTimeout for timers, removeEventListener for scroll handlers). The scroll listener uses { passive: true } for performance. No stale closures or leaked listeners.

add.header: No unsafe type patterns in source code
add.description: Despite missing strict mode, the codebase has zero 'any' annotations, zero 'as any' casts, zero '// @ts-ignore' comments, and zero '// type: ignore' comments. The developer writes types correctly by convention, even though the compiler doesn't enforce strictness.

tsconfig.app.json omits 'strict: true', so null/undefined are silently assignable to all typed variables. This is a configuration gap rather than a code quality issue — the code itself is typed correctly, but the compiler won't catch null-safety violations. This is the single most impactful type_safety finding and the main cap on the score.

add.header: Public API functions lack return type annotations
add.description: The three exported functions (App, Button, cn) all lack explicit return type annotations. While their return types are trivially inferred (JSX.Element or string), explicit annotations would make the public API contract self-documenting and prevent accidental signature drift during refactoring.

The codebase consistently uses the 'type' keyword for type-only imports (type VariantProps, type ReactNode, type ClassValue), which is correct for the verbatimModuleSyntax setting and avoids unnecessary runtime imports.
